newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania Jews cite two lists of Holocaust accounts.
newsitem.headline: Romania Jews cite two lists of Holocaust accounts.

text.p: Romanian Jews on Wednesday welcomed the publication by Swiss banks of a list of Holocaust-era account holders, including 49 from Romania, and said they had been given a separate list with 23 other holders.
"The publication of the list is a very wise measure, but we have to wait to see what will come of it," Iulian Sorin, Secretary of the Federation of Romania's Jewish Communities, said by telephone.
The list of more than 2,000 foreigners who held accounts in Switzerland before World War Two was published in newspapers in 28 countries, including the Bucharest daily Libertatea.

Forty-nine of the accounts were in the name of Romanian residents and companies. Some names appeared to indicate that the holders were Jews, others were Romanian or apparently members of the large ethnic German community.
Claimants were asked to call the offices of the international accounting firm Ernst and Young in neighbouring Hungary or one of five other offices elsewhere.

The second list, composed solely of Jewish account holders, was printed last month with scant publicity in two newspapers -- the Bucharest Jewish community's Realitatea Evreiasca (Jewish Reality) and Israel's Romanian-language Ultima Ora.

Published at the bottom of page two of the Bucharest publication under the title "Important Announcement", the item asked readers to contact the newspaper to enable international bodies to hand back the money.

A journalist within Romania's Jewish community, reduced to 14,000 members from 800,000 before the war, said the list was also compiled by Swiss banks and brought to Romania. He said the total deposited by the holders was unknown.
"The accounts opened by Romanian Jews in Swiss banks ranged from 1,500 to 30,000 Swiss francs at the time, depending on how well off they were," Peter Sragher told Reuters.
"There must have been many more accounts than those on the two lists. But so many Jews left communist Romania that some must have recovered their money and closed the accounts."

He said two relatives of Simon Docteur, one of the 23 account holders, had already stepped forward to claim the money in the account, estimated now to value 80,000 Swiss francs. Both were Romanian Jews long settled in Israel.

Among the 23 holders were names from a part of the former Soviet republic of Ukraine once held by Romania and two from Moldova -- also formerly part of the Soviet Union and a Romanian province between the two world wars.

The Holocaust and subsequent mass emigration wiped out 510 Jewish communities throughout Romania. Half of the Balkan country's 800,000 Jews perished in Nazi death camps and 320,000 of the survivors emigrated under communist rule, some "sold" by dictator Nicolae Ceausescu in the 1970s.

Seven years after the collapse of communist rule, Romanian authorities are only just beginning to restore property to the Jewish community. This includes hundreds of synagogues, former hospitals, ritual baths and other buildings. ($ = 1.483 Swiss Francs)
